title: X-ray Spectra
short_intro: X-ray spectra consist of a continuous bremsstrahlung background produced by the deceleration of high-speed electrons and characteristic line spectra arising from electronic transitions between inner atomic shells. These high-energy electromagnetic radiations follow Moseley's law, connecting frequency to atomic number.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Continuous and characteristic X-rays, Coolidge tube working, Duane-Hunt law, minimum wavelength, and qualitative aspects of X-ray production.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Moseley's law derivation and application, fine structure of characteristic X-rays, screening constants, absorption edges, and Auger effect.

prerequisites: Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom and energy levels
Pauli's exclusion principle and inner shell electron configurations

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Continuous X-ray Spectra
bullets: Produced when high-energy electrons strike a heavy metal target and undergo sudden deceleration (bremsstrahlung) in the Coulomb field of target nuclei.
The energy of the emitted photon ranges from zero up to the maximum kinetic energy of the incident electron, E = eV.
The short-wavelength limit (cut-off wavelength) is independent of the target material and depends solely on the accelerating potential.

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Characteristic X-ray Spectra
bullets: Arises when an incident electron knocks out an inner-shell electron (K or L shell), creating a vacancy.
An electron from an outer shell jumps down to fill the vacancy, emitting a photon with energy equal to the difference between the two orbital energy levels.
The spectrum consists of sharp lines grouped into series named K, L, M, N based on the principal quantum number of the shell where the vacancy originated.

concept_notes.heading: Moseley's Law and Atomic Number
bullets: H.G.J. Moseley established that the square root of the frequency of a given characteristic X-ray line is directly proportional to the atomic number Z of the target element.
Expressed mathematically as sqrt(nu) = a(Z - b), where a is a proportionality constant and b is the screening constant.
Proved that atomic number, rather than atomic weight, is the fundamental property governing the chemical and physical identity of elements.

concept_notes.heading: Fine Structure and X-ray Notation
bullets: Characteristic lines are designated using Siegbahn notation (Ka1, Ka2, Kb1, etc.) or IUPAC notation.
Transitions into the K shell from L_II and L_III subshells give rise to the doublet Ka2 and Ka1, explained by spin-orbit coupling.
Selection rules for X-ray transitions follow quantum mechanics: delta(l) = +-1 and delta(j) = 0, +-1.

derivations.title: Duane-Hunt Law for Minimum Wavelength
derivations.conditions: Electron accelerated through potential V striking a target
steps: Equate the maximum kinetic energy of the incident electron to the maximum energy of the emitted X-ray photon.
Substitute frequency relation \nu_{max} = \frac{c}{\lambda_{min}} into the energy equation.

derivations.title: Moseley's Law Frequency Derivation
derivations.conditions: Transition of an electron between principal quantum numbers n_2 and n_1 in a multielectron atom
steps: Use Bohr's energy expression modified for an effective nuclear charge Z_{eff} = Z - b.
Write the energy difference for the transition from n_2 to n_1: \Delta E = h \nu = E_{n2} - E_{n1}.
Take the square root of both sides to obtain a linear relation with (Z - b).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Continuous and Characteristic X-ray Spectrum
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Intensity (y-axis) vs Wavelength (x-axis) showing a sharp cut-off at lambda_min, a continuous background curve peaking at higher wavelengths, and sharp characteristic peaks superimposed.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The sharp cut-off represents maximum photon energy from electron deceleration. Sharp peaks represent discrete electronic transitions in inner shells.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions test the dependence of lambda_min on accelerating voltage and the independence of characteristic peak positions from voltage.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Moseley's Plot (sqrt(nu) vs Z)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Straight line plot of sqrt(nu) on the y-axis against atomic number Z on the x-axis for K_alpha lines, with a small positive intercept on the Z axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms the linear relationship predicted by Moseley's law, validating the atomic number concept over atomic mass.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested for identifying slopes, screening constants, or finding unknown atomic numbers from frequency data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Coolidge Tube Experimental Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Evacuated glass bulb with a heated cathode filament, focusing cup, high-voltage DC supply across terminals, and a cooled heavy metal anode (tungsten) inclined at 45 degrees.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the conversion of electrical energy into thermal energy and X-ray radiation, highlighting water cooling to prevent target melting.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on the role of filament current (controls intensity) and accelerating voltage (controls hardness/wavelength).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced by an X-ray tube operating at an accelerating potential of 40 kV.
solution_steps: Identify given values: V = 40 kV = 40 \times 10^3 V, h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} J s, c = 3 \times 10^8 m/s, e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} C.

solved_numericals.question: Using Moseley's law sqrt(\nu) = a(Z - b), find the frequency of the K_alpha line for an element with atomic number Z = 41, given constant a = 4.95 \times 10^7 Hz^{1/2} and screening constant b = 1 for the K shell.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: Z = 41, b = 1, a = 4.95 \times 10^7 Hz^{1/2}.
Calculate effective atomic number: Z - b = 41 - 1 = 40.
Calculate square root of frequency: \sqrt{\nu} = (4.95 \times 10^7) \times 40 = 1.98 \times 10^9 Hz^{1/2}.
Square both sides to find frequency: \nu = (1.98 \times 10^9)^2 = 3.92 \times 10^{18} Hz.

solved_numericals.question: In a Coolidge tube, if the accelerating potential is increased from 20 kV to 40 kV, what is the ratio of the minimum wavelength of continuous X-rays produced?
solution_steps: Recall Duane-Hunt law: \lambda_{min} is inversely proportional to accelerating voltage V, i.e., \lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}.
Substitute given voltages: V_1 = 20 kV and V_2 = 40 kV.

assumptions_and_limitations: Moseley's simple screening formula assumes single-electron transitions from the L to K shell, ignoring complex multi-electron screening interactions in higher shells.
The Duane-Hunt limit assumes all kinetic energy of a single incident electron is converted into a single photon in a single collision.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The characteristic X-ray wavelength depends on the accelerating voltage of the tube.
common_misconceptions.correct: Characteristic X-ray wavelengths depend only on the target material's atomic structure.
common_misconceptions.why: Accelerating voltage only determines whether the inner shell electron can be knocked out; once emitted, the line wavelength is governed by atomic energy levels.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Continuous X-ray spectra are produced by electronic transitions between discrete atomic energy levels.
common_misconceptions.correct: Continuous X-rays are produced by bremsstrahlung radiation due to deceleration of electrons.
common_misconceptions.why: Energy loss is continuous during deceleration in the nuclear Coulomb field, unlike discrete transitions.

quick_revision: Minimum wavelength lambda_min = hc / (eV) depends solely on the accelerating potential V.
Minimum X-ray Wavelength (Duane-Hunt Law): \lambda_{min} = \frac{h c}{e V}
